claims.text: The patient presented to the emergency department on 05/01/26 with sudden severe central chest pain rated 8/10, described as sharp and exacerbated by deep breaths and movement, with onset approximately one hour prior to arrival.
Associated symptoms included mild shortness of breath; the patient denied haemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, syncope, dysphagia, dysuria, haematuria, focal weakness, or dizziness.
Past medical history includes asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis.
The patient has a known allergy to pollen.
The patient reported no current medications at presentation.
Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent with activities of daily living, works as an IT consultant, and is a non-smoker with no alcohol or recreational drug use.
Family history is reported as nil significant.
Initial observations on 05/01/26 recorded a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24/min, temperature of 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation of 95-96% on room air.
Physical examination on 05/01/26 revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and palpable subcutaneous crepitus in the neck and anterior chest wall, with clear breath sounds and no added sounds.
An ECG performed at 02:30 on 05/01/26 showed sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic changes.
A chest X-ray performed on 05/01/26 confirmed spontaneous pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema, with no evidence of pneumothorax.
The clinical impression was spontaneous pneumomediastinum, likely secondary to a recent coughing episode or straining, with no evidence of haemodynamic instability.
Initial management on 05/01/26 included admission to the respiratory high-dependency unit, paracetamol 1g four times daily for pain, and ibuprofen 400mg three times daily for pain.
The patient was advised to avoid straining, heavy lifting, and activities that increase intrathoracic pressure.

Physiotherapy sessions on 05/01/26 and 06/01/26 focused on diaphragmatic breathing and pursed-lip breathing techniques to reduce respiratory strain, with the patient instructed to practice exercises every two hours while awake.

Observations during the physiotherapy assessment on 05/01/26 at 11:00 showed a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 20/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air.

On 05/01/26, observations showed a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, with examination noting no subcutaneous emphysema on palpation.
Omeprazole 20mg once daily was started on 05/01/26 to prevent gastrointestinal side effects from ibuprofen.
A repeat chest X-ray on 06/01/26 demonstrated a slight reduction in pneumomediastinum compared to initial imaging.
On 07/01/26, the patient reported no chest pain overnight and mild improvement in breathing comfort, with examination showing no palpable subcutaneous crepitus.
Regular paracetamol and ibuprofen were stopped on 07/01/26 as the patient was pain-free.
A repeat chest X-ray was planned for 48 hours after the 06/01/26 scan to assess further resolution.
On 07/01/26, the patient received education regarding signs of pneumomediastinum recurrence and when to seek urgent medical attention post-discharge.

On 08/01/26, observations recorded a heart rate of 82 bpm, blood pressure of 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate of 16/min, temperature of 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 97% on air, with examination showing no subcutaneous crepitus and clear chest.
Discharge planning was initiated on 08/01/26, including contact with the patient's GP to ensure continuity of care and arrangement of routine outpatient follow-up in the respiratory clinic.
A final chest X-ray reviewed on 09/01/26 showed complete resolution of spontaneous pneumomediastinum with no subcutaneous emphysema or abnormalities.
The patient was cleared for discharge on 09/01/26 with no further imaging required.
